units.text: Preparing for the Migration: Companionship, Two Mounts, and Provisions
How did waiting for permission turn into preparations for companionship, two riding animals, and provisions in Abu Bakr’s household?

Some Muslims had already headed for Medina, and Abu Bakr had prepared to leave. But the Prophet ﷺ asked him to wait: he hoped to receive permission himself. Abu Bakr remained in hope of accompanying him and prepared two riding animals. Then the Prophet ﷺ came to Abu Bakr’s house at an hour when he did not usually visit them, bringing news of permission to depart.

The story does not end with the decision to leave. The report describes an offer of a mount and the reply “at its price.” ‘A’isha then recounts the preparation of provisions in the plural, while Asma herself describes how she used her waistband to tie the travel bag and waterskin. Each account has its own setting and voice.
Waiting While Preparing

‘A’isha relates that the Prophet ﷺ told the Muslims of the place of their migration, with palm trees between two lava tracts, and those who migrated headed for Medina. Abu Bakr too had prepared to go there, but the Prophet ﷺ told him, “Wait a little, for I hope to receive permission.” Abu Bakr asked whether he expected that; when he answered yes, Abu Bakr held himself back to accompany him.

Waiting also meant working: Abu Bakr fed the two riding animals in his care leaves of the samur tree, called khabat in the report, for four months. Ibn Ishaq says he bought the two animals and kept them at his house, feeding them in preparation.
A Visit at an Unusual Hour

‘A’isha relates that they were at Abu Bakr’s house at midday when someone told her father that the Messenger of God ﷺ was approaching with his head covered, at an hour when he never visited them. Abu Bakr understood that the visit at that time signaled something important. The Prophet ﷺ asked permission to enter, then asked that those with Abu Bakr leave; Abu Bakr said they were his family. The Prophet then told him, “I have been given permission to depart.”
Abu Bakr asked about accompanying him, and the Prophet ﷺ answered yes. In the account of ‘A’isha cited by Ibn Ishaq in Ibn Hisham’s Sira, ‘A’isha says she saw Abu Bakr weep for joy that day.
The Mount at Its Price

Abu Bakr offered the Prophet ﷺ one of the two mounts. In ‘A’isha’s report in al-Bukhari, the brief reply was “At its price.” In Ibn Ishaq’s narrative, when the two mounts were brought, Abu Bakr offered the better one. The Prophet ﷺ would not ride a camel he did not own; he asked its purchase price and took it at that price.
The Provisions and What Asma Did

‘A’isha relates: “We equipped them as quickly as we could, and made them provisions for the journey in a leather bag.” She then specifies what Asma bint Abi Bakr did: she cut a piece from her waistband and tied it around the bag’s mouth. The sufra here means provisions for a journey, and the jirab is their bag; this excerpt does not identify what the provisions consisted of.

Asma, for her part, says in the first person that she made the Messenger of God’s travel provisions ﷺ at Abu Bakr’s house. She says they could find nothing with which to tie the provisions and the waterskin. When she mentioned her waistband to her father, he told her to split it in two and tie the waterskin with one half and the provisions with the other; she did so. The waistband was what she tied around her waist. Her report ends with the name “the woman of the two waistbands.”

The provisions appear again in Ibn Ishaq’s narrative as they prepare to leave after staying in the cave: Asma brought them but had forgotten to provide a strap for hanging them, so she made her waistband into a strap.
What Does ‘A’isha Tell Us, and What Does Asma Tell Us?

‘A’isha’s “we equipped them” includes participants in the preparations without naming each of them or saying that she personally carried the provisions to the cave. She then names Asma’s action in tying the bag. In Asma’s fuller account, she attributes to herself the making of the provisions in her father’s house and mentions the waterskin too. We can read both contributions without turning the plural into one person’s act or omitting the waterskin from Asma’s testimony.

‘A’isha mentions provisions in a bag and tying a piece of the waistband around its mouth, and gives the title “the woman of the waistband.” In her fuller account, Asma describes splitting the waistband to tie the waterskin and provisions, and gives “the woman of the two waistbands.” We must not make the bag and waterskin the same object or write the two titles as though both reports used identical words.
Between the Narrative and Ibn Hisham’s Comment

Ibn Ishaq’s narrative in Ibn Hisham’s Sira ends the scene of the provisions’ arrival with the title “the woman of the waistband.” Ibn Hisham then says he heard more than one scholar call her “the woman of the two waistbands” and explains that Asma hung the provisions from half her waistband and wore the other half around her waist. This is Ibn Hisham’s explanation, not Asma’s own words, and differs from Asma’s fuller statement about tying the waterskin and provisions with the two pieces.
Limits of Time and Money

The four months in ‘A’isha’s report describe feeding the two riding animals; on their own, they cannot establish the journey’s duration. Ibn Ishaq’s account gives the price of the mount as “such and such,” not a fixed amount. These passages do not explain why payment was chosen. The dialogue is intelligible without supplying a number or an explanation from outside the readings.

In Asma’s account, transmitted by Ibn Ishaq through Yahya ibn ‘Abbad, his father, and his grandmother Asma, she says that after the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr departed, her father took all his wealth with him, “five thousand dirhams or six thousand.” Her grandfather Abu Quhafa, who had lost his sight, worried about those left in the house. She placed stones in a wall recess, covered them, and showed him where they were to reassure him. At the end she says explicitly that Abu Bakr had left them nothing and that she meant to comfort the old man. This is an account of the departure’s effect on the household, not an estimate of the mount’s price; the uncertainty between the two sums remains.
Migrants head for Medina; Abu Bakr awaits companionship and feeds the two mounts.
The midday visit brings news of permission and the question of companionship.
The mount is offered and accepted at a price, not as a gift without payment.
‘A’isha recounts preparation in the plural; Asma recounts making and tying the provisions.
In Ibn Ishaq’s narrative, Asma brings the provisions when they depart.
‘A’isha’s account: waiting and feeding the two mounts — al-Bukhari
Buying the two mounts in Ibn Ishaq’s account
‘A’isha’s account: the midday visit, permission, and price — al-Bukhari
‘A’isha’s account according to Ibn Ishaq: from the visit to the joy
The price dialogue in Ibn Ishaq’s narrative and its continuation on the next page
‘A’isha: preparations, the bag, and a piece of the waistband
Asma: the provisions, waterskin, and split waistband
Ibn Ishaq’s narrative: the provisions arrive, followed by the variant titles
Asma and her grandfather Abu Quhafa: money and stones
Distinguish the Muslims’ departure from the waiting for companionship in the words presented.
Distinguish the period of preparing the two mounts from the period of travel and the stay.
Read the relative time and recognize what was unusual about this visit without inventing an exact hour.
Identify who asked to accompany whom and who replied, according to the text.
Distinguish what ‘A’isha reports about joy from what a later narrator might compose.
Distinguish accepting a mount for its price from assuming a number or accepting a gift.
Distinguish the plural in ‘A’isha’s report from Asma’s own attributed actions.
Preserve the variant titles and details of what was tied, without conflating their wording.
Distinguish Ibn Hisham’s comment from the conclusion of Ibn Ishaq’s narrative.
Preserve the uncertainty between two amounts; do not take an act of reassurance as proof of money left behind.
How did the course of those Muslims who migrated differ from Abu Bakr’s position in ‘A’isha’s account?
The departure of some Muslims for Medina does not negate the Prophet’s waiting for permission ﷺ or Abu Bakr’s holding back to accompany him.
According to ‘A’isha’s passage in al-Bukhari, not an enumeration of all migrants.
Those who migrated did so; the Prophet ﷺ asked Abu Bakr to wait, and he held himself back in hope of accompanying him.
Yes: some Muslims began migrating while Abu Bakr waited to accompany him.
All the Muslims waited until Abu Bakr left first.
The text mentions the departure of some migrants before Abu Bakr remained behind waiting.
Abu Bakr prevented the Muslims from migrating until the Prophet ﷺ received permission.
The report says nothing of preventing others; only that Abu Bakr himself waited.
What activity do the “four months” refer to in the account of the two mounts?
Observe where the duration appears: “he fed two riding animals ... for four months.”
Do not turn the preparation period into the length of the journey.
Abu Bakr feeding the two mounts samur leaves.
Correct: the duration follows the description of feeding them.
The journey from Mecca to Medina.
The report does not make it the journey’s length; it follows the feeding of the mounts.
Their stay in the cave.
This is the time spent feeding them before departure, not the stay in the cave.
What made the Prophet’s arrival ﷺ at Abu Bakr’s house noteworthy in ‘A’isha’s account?
The description of the time and “at an hour when he did not come to us” explain why Abu Bakr inferred that something had prompted the visit.
The person who alerted Abu Bakr is not named in this excerpt.
He came at the height of midday, at an hour when he did not usually visit them.
Correct: the unusual time is what marks the visit in the report.
He arrived with the two mounts at the door.
This passage does not say he brought the mounts.
He sent a messenger whom the report names instead of coming himself.
The person announced that the Prophet ﷺ was coming; the Prophet then asked permission to enter and came in.
Who asked to accompany the other after permission to depart was announced, and what was the reply?
The request for companionship comes between the announcement of permission and Abu Bakr’s offer of a mount.
In the selected passage from al-Bukhari.
Abu Bakr asked and the Prophet ﷺ answered yes.
Correct: Abu Bakr asked and the Prophet ﷺ replied.
‘A’isha asked, and Abu Bakr answered her yes.
‘A’isha reports the conversation; she is not the person asking in it.
The Prophet ﷺ asked about companionship, and Abu Bakr declined.
In the text Abu Bakr asks and the reply is yes.
Who reports Abu Bakr’s tears of joy in Ibn Ishaq’s account in Ibn Hisham?
The reading moves from Ibn Ishaq’s chain to ‘A’isha’s words, which identify who described the tears of joy.
The tears appear in Ibn Hisham’s continuation, not in the selected excerpt from al-Bukhari.
‘A’isha, who says she saw him weeping that day.
Correct: the text attributes this observation to ‘A’isha.
Ibn Hisham, as an eyewitness present in Abu Bakr’s house.
Ibn Hisham transmits ‘A’isha’s account and does not describe himself as a witness to the visit.
The unnamed person who announced the Prophet’s arrival ﷺ.
That person appears in al-Bukhari’s account of the visit, not as the narrator of the tears here.
What does the price dialogue in Ibn Ishaq establish, without adding anything from outside it?
The answer “such and such” rules out supplying a specific amount, although the decision to take the mount for a price is clear.
Read the Ibn Ishaq narrative presented here; do not fill in the amount from another report.
The Prophet ﷺ asked what the mount had cost and took it at that price; the amount is given only as “such and such.”
Yes: the dialogue establishes payment without specifying a number.
He accepted the mount as a gift without asking its price.
The text describes the offer as a gift, then its rejection and the question about price.
Abu Bakr gave an exact numerical amount preserved in the excerpt.
The reply preserved here is “such and such,” with no number.
Which description preserves the difference between the two speakers’ pronouns in the preparation accounts?
‘A’isha’s use of the plural does not mean she named every participant, and Asma’s own action does not erase that plural.
Read each woman’s words in her own text, not a composite of the two.
‘A’isha says “we equipped them” in the plural; Asma says “I made the provisions” in her own voice.
Correct: this preserves both the plural and Asma’s direct action.
‘A’isha alone says “I made the provisions,” and Asma does not mention her work.
“I made” comes from Asma’s account; ‘A’isha’s uses the plural.
Both accounts attribute making the provisions solely to ‘A’isha in the singular.
Asma’s account uses the first-person singular; ‘A’isha’s uses the plural.
What difference between ‘A’isha’s and Asma’s accounts of tying the waistband should we preserve?
In ‘A’isha’s excerpt, “the woman of the waistband” accompanies a piece tied to the bag’s mouth; in Asma’s account, “the woman of the two waistbands” accompanies splitting it to tie two containers.
Do not assume the containers are the same or the titles identically worded.
‘A’isha mentions a piece tied around the bag’s mouth; Asma mentions splitting the waistband to tie the waterskin and provisions.
Correct: the detail about the waterskin belongs to Asma’s account, not ‘A’isha’s excerpt.
‘A’isha describes two pieces for the waterskin and provisions; Asma mentions only the bag’s mouth.
This reverses which account gives which details.
Both describe tying only the waterskin, with no provisions or bag.
Both readings address the provisions; Asma also specifies the waterskin.
In Ibn Hisham’s continuation of the provisions scene, where does his distinct voice appear, as opposed to Ibn Ishaq’s narrative?
The reading separates the end of Ibn Ishaq’s narrative from “Ibn Hisham said” and the report and interpretation that follow.
Do not present Ibn Hisham’s explanation as Asma’s wording in her fuller account.
In his statement that he heard more than one scholar say “the woman of the two waistbands,” followed by his explanation of splitting the waistband.
Correct: his comment follows the title at the end of the earlier narrative.
In Asma’s words “I made the provisions” as reported by al-Bukhari.
Those are Asma’s words in another reading, not Ibn Hisham’s comment.
In the sentence ending Ibn Ishaq’s narrative with “the woman of the waistband.”
That ends the narrative before Ibn Hisham’s comment.
How does Asma explain placing stones where her father’s money might have been after his departure?
Her initial words to her grandfather were meant to reassure him, not to prove that money remained in the recess; the uncertainty between the two sums remains.
In Asma’s account transmitted by Ibn Ishaq through Yahya ibn ‘Abbad from his father.
She wanted to soothe her worried grandfather and says her father left them nothing.
Correct: Asma ends by explaining her purpose.
The stones were money Abu Bakr left for her grandfather to spend.
Asma explicitly says they were stones and that her father left them nothing.
She wanted to prove that the amount was five thousand, not six.
The account wavers between five and six thousand; the stones do not prove either sum.

“Such and such” cannot establish the price of the mount, nor does Asma’s account resolve the uncertainty about the amount Abu Bakr carried. Both estimates and phrases must remain attributed to their respective speakers.

The Prophet ﷺ was then in Mecca. He said to the Muslims, “I have been shown the place of your migration, a place of palms between two stony lava tracts.” Those who migrated went toward Medina, and most of those who had migrated to Abyssinia returned to Medina. Abu Bakr also prepared to go to Medina, but the Messenger of God ﷺ said to him, “Take your time, for I hope to receive permission.” Abu Bakr said, “Do you hope for that? May my father be your ransom.” He said, “Yes.” So Abu Bakr held himself back to accompany the Messenger of God ﷺ and fed two riding animals he had leaves of the samur tree, which are called khabat, for four months.

Ibn Ishaq

Ibn Ishaq said: Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, was a man of means. When he asked the Messenger of God ﷺ for permission to migrate, the Messenger of God ﷺ said, “Do not hurry. Perhaps God will provide you a companion.” Abu Bakr hoped that the Messenger of God ﷺ meant himself by this. He bought two riding animals and kept them in his house, feeding them in preparation.

Ibn Shihab said: ‘Urwa said: ‘A’isha said: One day, while we were sitting in Abu Bakr’s house at the height of midday, someone said to Abu Bakr, “Here is the Messenger of God ﷺ, with his head covered, at an hour when he does not usually come to us.” Abu Bakr said, “May my father and mother be his ransom! By God, something important must have brought him at this hour.” She said: The Messenger of God ﷺ arrived and asked permission to enter; permission was given and he came in. The Prophet ﷺ said to Abu Bakr, “Send those with you out.” Abu Bakr said, “They are your family, may my father be your ransom, Messenger of God.” He said, “I have been given permission to depart.” Abu Bakr said, “To accompany you? May my father be your ransom, Messenger of God?” The Messenger of God ﷺ said, “Yes.” Abu Bakr said, “Then take one of these two riding animals of mine, may my father be your ransom, Messenger of God.” The Messenger of God ﷺ replied, “At its price.”

The Messenger of God ﷺ never failed to come to Abu Bakr’s house at one end of the day, either morning or evening. But on the day he was given permission to migrate and leave Mecca from among his people, the Messenger of God ﷺ came to us at midday, at an hour when he did not usually come. God ﷺ sat down. Only my sister Asma bint Abi Bakr and I were with Abu Bakr. The Messenger of God ﷺ said, “Send away those with you.” Abu Bakr replied, “Messenger of God, they are only my two daughters [1]. What is it? May my father and mother be your ransom!” He said, “God has given me permission to depart and migrate.” Abu Bakr said, “Companionship, Messenger of God?” He said, “Companionship.” By God, before that day I had never realized someone could weep for joy, until I saw Abu Bakr weeping that day. Then he said, “Prophet of God, these are two riding animals I have prepared for this.” They hired ‘Abd Allah ibn Arqat, a man of Banu al-Du’il ibn Bakr whose mother was of Banu Sahm ibn ‘Amr and who was a polytheist, to guide them along the way. They entrusted their two mounts to him; he cared for them until their appointed time.

The Messenger of God ﷺ replied, “I do not ride a camel that is not mine.” He said, “Then it is yours, Messenger of God, may my father and mother be your ransom.” He said, “No. What price did you buy it for?” He said, “Such and such.” He said, “I have taken it for that price.” He replied, “It is yours, Messenger of God [1].” They mounted and departed, and Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may God be pleased with him, took his freedman ‘Amir ibn Fuhayra riding behind him to serve them on the road.

“I made the Messenger of God’s travel provisions ﷺ in Abu Bakr’s house when he intended to migrate to Medina. We could find nothing to tie his provisions and his waterskin with. I said to Abu Bakr, ‘By God, I cannot find anything to tie them with except my waistband.’ He said, ‘Split it in two: tie the waterskin with one piece and the provisions with the other.’ I did so, and for this I was called ‘the woman of the two waistbands.’”

Ibn Ishaq said: The Messenger of God ﷺ stayed in the cave for three days with Abu Bakr. Quraysh offered a hundred she-camels to anyone who brought him back to them after he disappeared. ‘Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr spent the daytime among Quraysh, hearing what they plotted and said about the Messenger of God ﷺ and Abu Bakr; at night he would go to them and give them the news. ‘Amir ibn Fuhayra, Abu Bakr’s freedman, tended livestock among the shepherds of Mecca. In the evening he drove Abu Bakr’s sheep to the two men, and they milked and slaughtered. When ‘Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr left them for Mecca in the morning, ‘Amir ibn Fuhayra followed his tracks with the sheep to erase them. Once the three days had passed and the people ceased pursuing them, the man they had hired came to them with their two camels and one of his own. Asma bint Abi Bakr, may God be pleased with them both, brought them their travel provisions, but she had forgotten to provide a strap. When they prepared to set out, she went to hang up the provisions and found there was no strap [1]. She untied her waistband, made it into a strap, and hung them with it.

She said: When the Messenger of God ﷺ departed, with Abu Bakr alongside him, Abu Bakr took all his wealth; he had five thousand dirhams or six thousand with him, and took it along. My grandfather Abu Quhafa, whose sight had gone, came to us and said, “By God, I do not think he has hurt you by taking his money as well as himself.” [Translator’s note: the supplied text reads «إنِّي لَا أَرَاهُ»; the negation is unclear in this context.] I said, “No, father! He left us much good.” I took some stones, put them in a recess in the house where my father used to keep his money, and covered them with a cloth. I took his hand and said, “Father, place your hand on this money.” He placed his hand on it and said, “That is all right. If he has left you this, he has done well; this will be enough for you.” But, by God, he left us nothing. I only wanted to reassure the old man.

review.summary: Internal AI bilingual semantic comparison attested by reviewer session 2bd6716d-fdb0-4362-872d-81e2b1f40eab across 235 Arabic/target units. Compared every one of the 235 paired teaching, question/answer, metadata and full selected source-text units directly against the bound Arabic in all ten untruncated pairs.py chunks. Checked the Arabic watchlist, distinct speakers and chains, quotation limits, chronology, uncertainty, citations and source-reading completeness.
